story.hook: My boss demanded unpaid overtime, so I asked him to confirm the rule by email. That email ended the policy before lunch.
story.script:
My boss demanded unpaid overtime, so I asked him to confirm the rule by email. That email ended the policy before lunch.

We were three days from month-end when my manager called a last-minute team meeting. He said our department was behind target, so everyone was now expected to stay from six until eight every evening for the rest of the month. Then he added the important part: nobody should submit overtime because, according to him, ‘being committed means doing what the team needs.’

The room went quiet. A few people looked annoyed, but nobody argued. I had joined the department only a few months earlier, and during onboarding we had been told that extra hours had to be recorded accurately, even when a manager thought they should not be paid. I did not want to start a public fight, so I asked one simple question: was this a request, or was it mandatory?

He said it was mandatory. He also said anyone leaving at the normal time would be remembered during performance reviews.

After the meeting, I went back to my desk and wrote a very boring email. I thanked him for clarifying the month-end arrangement and asked him to confirm four things so I could plan my schedule: that the extra two hours were mandatory, that we were not allowed to submit overtime, that the rule applied to the whole team, and that leaving at the normal time could affect our performance rating.

I expected him to soften the wording. Instead, he replied almost immediately: ‘Correct on all points. Please make sure everyone complies.’

That reply made things much easier.

Our time-entry system had a help address for payroll questions, so I forwarded the thread and asked how I was supposed to record mandatory hours if my manager had instructed us not to submit them. I did not accuse anyone of anything. I just attached his answer and asked which code I should use.

About twenty minutes later, payroll copied in HR. Ten minutes after that, HR asked me not to change anything in the email thread and said they were reviewing the instruction.

Then my manager disappeared into a meeting.

While he was gone, everyone kept working, but the team chat was suddenly very active. Nobody knew exactly what was happening until an HR representative joined our department call just before lunch.

She said there had been a misunderstanding about month-end coverage. All working time still had to be recorded. Any approved overtime would be handled under the normal policy. Nobody could be penalized for refusing unrecorded extra hours, and managers were not allowed to tell staff to hide time worked.

My manager came back on camera looking like he had aged a week in forty minutes. He said the evening requirement was cancelled ‘to avoid confusion.’

That would already have been enough, but HR was not finished. They reviewed the previous month as well and found that several teammates had stayed late without recording the hours because they had been given the same verbal instruction before I joined. Payroll contacted those employees individually to correct their records.

The funniest part came that afternoon. My manager sent the team a new email reminding us that accurate time reporting was ‘extremely important’ and that all instructions should follow company policy.

Nobody replied for a while.

Then one coworker reacted with a thumbs-up.

By the end of the day, we were all leaving at our normal time, the old unpaid hours were being reviewed, and the new ‘mandatory’ policy had lasted less than four hours.

I never had to argue with my boss. I just asked him to put the rule in writing, and he did the rest himself.

youtube.title: I Asked My Boss to Put the Overtime Rule in Writing #Shorts
youtube.description: A manager tried to make unpaid overtime mandatory. One confirmation email made the rule collapse before lunch. An original Wacky Dramas story.
